## Linux: root no longer follows or waits on what the service account puts in /etc/observer

**Mostly Linux (.deb).** On Windows, the package changes in its version number and in a few small things, listed at the end.

**What was wrong.** `sudo observer share`, `rotate-key` and `doctor` run as root inside `/etc/observer`, which belongs to the `observer` account the service runs as. They read `credentials.json` and `certificate.pfx` with the ordinary file calls. An attacker who had already taken over that account could put something else where those files belong. Measured with 0.24.4 run as root: a FIFO made the command wait for ever, a link to `/dev/zero` made it run out of memory, a socket ended in an unhandled exception, and a link to a file only root can read was read as root. When that file happened to be shaped like the store, `share` printed its secret, and a plain `rotate-key` (not `--now`) copied it into `previous` in the new store, which the `observer` account can read. Nothing in the package made the account easier to take over; this closes what root did once it had been.

**What changes.** Root opens each file once, never through a link at the file's own name, asks the open file what it is, and only then reads it, up to 64 KiB. A link, a FIFO, a device, a directory, a socket or a file over 64 KiB is refused with a sentence that says which, and nothing of it is read. So is a file with a second name (a hard link) that belongs to another account than the folder; the service's own file with a backup name next to it is read as before. `rotate-key` writes nothing when it refuses, and says that nothing was rotated. `doctor` says that what is where the store belongs is not a regular file, is over 64 KiB, or has a second name of another account, and offers no `chown` for it, because a `chown` changes the file behind the other name too, which may be root's. It also waits at most its own time limit for the local channel, and reports a socket whose queue of connections is full as `STUCK`. The answer of the local channel is read up to 64 KiB, and control characters in what it says are shown as `?`. `share` and `rotate-key` refuse a token that holds a character a terminal acts on, and print nothing of it; the text of a damaged store's error, which may quote a key of the file, is shown without such characters too.

**`rotate-key --now` does not need what the old store holds.** It writes a store with nothing of the old one in it, so a link or a FIFO at that name, a store that cannot be parsed and one that holds something that is not a token no longer stop it: it says that the old store was not read, and replaces the name, never what a link pointed to. An access denied still stops it, because the write would fail for the same reason. A plain `rotate-key` carries the old key over and still refuses all of these.

**If a command now refuses.** If you made the link or the extra name yourself, the refusal is deliberate: read what it points at with `sudo cat <that file>`. If you did not, stop the service (`sudo systemctl stop observer`), look with `sudo ls -l /etc/observer`, remove what does not belong and start it again. Removing `credentials.json` makes the service create a new token, and every dashboard that holds the old one stops connecting until it is given the new one. Removing `certificate.pfx` makes it create a new certificate: the fingerprint changes, and `observer share` shows the new one. If the sentence says that nothing is known to be wrong with the file, this machine could not check it: do not delete it, look at it with the two commands the sentence gives, and report what `uname -m` and `uname -r` print.

**Unchanged.** The packaged service is not root and reads its own folder as before, and so does root in a folder that root owns. A service started by hand as root in a folder another account owns now refuses to start, with one sentence, when the store or the certificate is a file root will not read or could not check. A file that is not there is reported as before.

**On Windows**, `rotate-key --now` no longer stops on a store it cannot parse; `share` and `rotate-key` refuse a token that holds a control character; `rotate-key` says that nothing was rotated when it does not rotate; and the answer of the local channel is read up to 64 KiB. Nothing else changes.

**Not fixed here.** `rotate-key --now` and `doctor` talk to the running service through a socket in `/run/observer`, a folder the same account controls, so a taken-over account can answer for the service, and its answer still reads as a verdict. A FUSE file system mounted by that account (off by default on most systems) can lie about who owns a folder. With `fs.protected_hardlinks=0` (not the default on Debian and Ubuntu) a link count is only a snapshot. Only x86-64 was measured: on other architectures a wrong value of `O_NOFOLLOW` makes root refuse to read, and does not make it follow. A directory planted at `credentials.json.new` stops a rotation with the error the write gives. Until these have their own changes, treat "the old key is refused" as true only if you trust the service account.
